title: Israel Salanter
hook: the story is told that he used little water for ritual washing, so the water-carrier wasn't overburdened

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: middot, measures, and your line, traits are measures: too little, too much, or the right amount. Today, a rabbi who measured even his water.

Before eating bread, observant Jews wash their hands from a cup, pouring water over each hand and saying a blessing. A story is told about one rabbi at that cup. People watching him expected a famous teacher to pour generously, splash after splash, the way a devout person might. Instead he poured just a little, the least the law allowed, and set the cup down. Someone asked him why so little.
screen: `A CUP BEFORE THE BREAD.` → `HE POURED JUST A LITTLE.` → `SOMEONE ASKED WHY.`

segments.voice: Israel Salanter. Four turns. First, the answer. As the story is told, the water in that house was hauled up from a well by a water-carrier, bucket by bucket, on her back. Every extra splash at the cup was another trip to the well for someone else. So the rabbi said, in effect: I won't be pious at her expense. Second, why it surprised people. The Talmud praises generous washing. In tractate Shabbat, a rabbi says he washed with full handfuls of water and was given full handfuls of good. Pouring more was a real mitzvah, and here was a great teacher choosing less. He didn't skip the washing; he kept it at the measure the law requires, and moved the extra devotion to the person carrying the buckets. Third, the man. Salanter was a rabbi in Lithuania whom tradition calls the father of the Mussar movement. This story is Mussar in a single gesture. Here even piety has a measure. Fourth, the other stories. Before Passover, asked what to watch for in a matzah bakery, he is said to have pointed to the women doing the kneading and said, in effect, don't overwork them. Whether every detail happened just this way, these stories are how his students remembered him. They carry an ordinary question into an ordinary week: the long shower someone else cleans up after, the volunteer shift that leaves a coworker covering yours. Devotion is real, and so is the person who pays for it.
screen: `THE WATER CAME FROM A WELL.` · `THE TALMUD PRAISES PLENTY OF WATER.` · `EVEN PIETY HAS A MEASURE.` · `WATCH THE ONES WHO KNEAD.` · then, large: `NOT PIOUS AT OTHERS' EXPENSE.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing in your day that someone else made possible without being thanked: the person who cleans the office, drives the bus, cooks the meal, empties the bins. Picture their hands at work, then one thing you do, even a good thing, that adds to their load, and hold both pictures side by side; nothing to fix, just see the buckets. If you pray, bring that person before God by name; if not, simply hold them in your attention.
Israel Salanter. The rabbi tradition calls the father of the Mussar movement, remembered for pouring little water so the water-carrier would carry less. Today's word.
Your line: not pious at others' expense. The scale includes other people's backs. See you tomorrow.

notes: The washing story circulates in several versions (a water-carrier, a maidservant; at home or as a guest). The lesson makes the carrier a woman and frames it as 'as the story is told'; confirm or neutralize the detail.
Shabbat 62b (Rav Chisda: one who washes with abundant water is given abundant good) is paraphrased; confirm the reference.
The matzah-bakery story is told as 'people tell another one'; confirm it is fair to attribute to Salanter.
'Tradition calls him the father of the Mussar movement' and 'a rabbi in Lithuania': no dates given on purpose. Y3 day 970 used the shoemaker's-candle story, so it is avoided here.
